target: AG1’s claim that school dissection mainly uses animals that were already dead or are meat-industry byproducts, so it does not significantly harm wildlife or require killing animals for class.
objection: School dissection animals are mostly supplied through wild capture, and wild-catching harms local populations and biodiversity, so the activity is ethically and environmentally harmful rather than harmless use of dead byproducts.

target: AG1’s claim that because AP Biology, NGSS, and medical-school practices do not require dissection, animal dissection is unnecessary.
objection: Even if dissection is educationally useful, it is not required by major science standards or physician-training programs, so the lack of a mandate counts against claiming it is necessary for school biology.

target: AG1’s claim that real dissection is needed because alternatives do not teach as well.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach equally well or better than real-animal dissection, so alternatives can achieve the same learning goals without using animals.

target: AG2’s claim that wild-caught procurement makes school dissection environmentally and ethically unjustified.
objection: Typical school specimens are said to be overwhelmingly already dead or meat-industry byproducts, so the asserted wildlife and biodiversity harms from wild-catching are not well supported for ordinary school dissection.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives are educationally sufficient for all relevant biology learning goals.
objection: Alternatives may teach content, but they do not provide the same hands-on, tactile practice that real dissection gives for fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination.

target: AG2’s claim that because AP/NGSS do not require dissection, schools should not use it.
objection: Education standards set outcomes, not a single required method; a method can still be justified if it effectively helps meet the learning outcomes, even if it is not explicitly mandated.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives lack comparable tactile practice for fine motor and hand-eye skills.
objection: Tangible synthetic dissection alternatives are designed to be handled and manipulated, so they can provide tactile practice comparable to real dissection for those skills.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can replace dissection for critical thinking.
objection: Real specimens force students to interpret uncertain, unlabeled biological evidence, whereas simulations are often pre-labeled or overly guided, so alternatives usually provide less practice with evidence-based reasoning and critical thinking.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives do not create the same open-ended, inference-based reasoning tasks as real dissection.
objection: Many virtual and physical alternatives can be configured so labels are hidden and students must infer structures before feedback, making them open-ended and uncertainty-based like real dissection.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives match dissection on working with anatomical variability and measurement.
objection: Real dissection exposes students to authentic natural variation across specimens and requires direct physical measurement, which many standard models and simulations do not replicate as fully.

target: AG1’s assumption that school alternatives do not present realistic anatomical variability or comparable measurement tasks.
objection: Many synthetic anatomy tools are built from imaging or specimen data and include measurement features, so they can present realistic variability and require comparable measurement and identification work.

target: AG1’s claim that school dissection is mainly harmless because specimens are already-dead byproducts.
objection: The fact that many specimens are said to come from wild capture means school dissection is still tied to intentional taking or killing of animals for specimen supply.

target: AG2’s claim that school dissection is ethically and environmentally unjustified because it requires killing animals specifically for class.
objection: Using fetal pigs and other byproducts diverts material from landfills and suggests school dissection is not primarily causing new killing for the class purpose.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection specimens are not intentionally sourced through wild capture.
objection: Wild-caught animals are often taken specifically for the dissection supply chain, so the specimens can indeed be obtained by killing or capturing animals for that purpose.

target: AG2’s reliance on medical-school policy as evidence against school biology dissection.
objection: Medical training and introductory biology have different goals, so the fact that medical schools do not use animals for physician training does not determine whether school biology classes should use dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that AP Biology and NGSS not requiring dissection does not matter.
objection: Because dissection is not required by AP Biology or NGSS, it is not needed to meet the mandated learning outcomes, especially when alternatives can achieve those outcomes too.

target: AG2’s argument that school dissection is unnecessary because standards do not require it and alternatives can replace it.
objection: Standards specify outcomes, not methods; if dissection helps achieve important outcomes like hands-on skills and critical thinking, it can still be justified even if not mandated.

target: AG2’s claim that school dissection specimens are primarily wild-caught in ecologically significant numbers.
objection: Typical school specimens are said to come mostly from already-dead animals and meat-industry byproducts, so they do not inherently require widespread wild-catching.

target: AG1’s claim that school dissection does not significantly involve wild-caught animals.
objection: The asserted supply chain indicates that dissection animals are predominantly wild-caught, so school specimens are primarily sourced through wild capture rather than captive or incidental sources.

target: AG1’s claim that byproducts and already-dead specimens avoid ethical and environmental problems.
objection: If school specimens are commercially sourced from a chain dominated by wild-caught animals, then the activity still depends on ecologically harmful wild capture even if some specimens are byproducts.

target: AG2’s claim that there is evidence school specimens are obtained by killing or ecologically significant wild-catching specifically for class.
objection: Typical school dissection can rely on already-dead and byproduct animals, so it does not necessarily involve special killing or wild-catching for the class activity.

target: AG1’s claim that school specimens are not obtained through ecologically significant wild-catching.
objection: If school dissection uses the standard dissection-animal supply chain, then it is still overwhelmingly sourced from wild-caught animals, making the supply ecologically significant.

target: AG2’s claim that because dissection is not required by standards and alternatives exist, students should not dissect animals.
objection: Even if dissection is not mandated, it can still be worthwhile because it provides unique hands-on skill-building, critical thinking, and motivation that alternatives may not match.

target: AG1’s assumption that school alternatives do not provide tactile practice comparable to real dissection.
objection: Many school-available alternatives use physical, cuttable materials that students manipulate with dissection tools, so they do provide tactile practice comparable to real dissection for fine-motor outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that tactile synthetic models fully replace the skill-building value of real tissue dissection.
objection: Fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination are developed through manipulating biological tissue itself, so representational or model-based activities usually do not match real dissection’s educational value.

target: AG1’s claim that tactile models are not comparable to real dissection for fine-motor and hand-eye skills.
objection: Synthetic, hands-on models let students manipulate anatomy-like materials with tools, so they can provide the same kind of tactile practice needed for those skills.

target: AG2’s claim that real dissection adds no necessary educational value beyond alternatives.
objection: Real dissection still provides unique direct tissue manipulation and therefore can supply educational value beyond what representational alternatives usually offer.

target: AG1’s assumption that no school alternatives provide comparable tactile practice.
objection: Some school alternatives are physical, cuttable models manipulated with scalpels and forceps, so there is evidence that at least some alternatives do provide comparable tactile practice.

target: AG1’s claim that school dissection does not involve animals killed specifically for the class.
objection: If specimens come from the wild-caught dissection-animal supply chain, then animals are being taken or killed for the dissection purpose rather than merely using incidental remains.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection should continue because it uses byproducts and offers educational benefits.
objection: Because dissection can still impose serious avoidable ethical and environmental harms while alternatives can meet the same learning goals, those harms outweigh the claimed benefits.
